title: Blog 1
content:
Building Multi-Region Resiliency for AWS CloudFormation Custom Resource Deployment The main idea of this blog is to show how AWS CloudFormation custom resources can be made more reliable when they are deployed across multiple AWS Regions. The article focuses on solving common problems such as failures, retries, partial deployments, and inconsistent state between Regions.
Main Point CloudFormation custom resources are useful, but they can be risky in multi-Region environments. They allow teams to extend CloudFormation with custom logic, but they also introduce important reliability challenges. When a stack is deployed across multiple Regions, a failure in one Region, a timeout, or a delayed response can cause incomplete operations or inconsistent state. The blog explains that the main problem is not only availability, but also avoiding duplicate execution and ensuring safe recovery after failures.
Problems The blog highlights several important problems with multi-Region custom resource deployments:
CloudFormation does not provide built-in multi-Region coordination for custom resources. The same event may be processed by more than one Region, which can create duplicate side effects. There is no native distributed locking mechanism to ensure only one handler processes a given request. If the primary Region fails, there is no automatic failover built into the custom resource flow. Developers must handle idempotency carefully so retries do not cause accidental duplicates. Solution Approach The proposed solution is an active-active multi-Region architecture. In this approach, multiple Regions are prepared to handle events at the same time, but only one Region should process a given request. The architecture uses distributed state tracking and coordination mechanisms to prevent duplicate processing. It also includes retry logic, monitoring, and failover so that the system can recover automatically when one Region experiences issues. This makes the deployment flow more reliable and better suited for mission-critical workloads.
What I Can Learn From this blog, I can learn how to:
understand how custom resources work in CloudFormation design systems that are more resilient and safer during failures apply important concepts such as idempotency, retries, and monitoring improve my understanding of AWS services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS, and Step Functions Read the original AWS blog

title: Blog 2
content:
Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS: Cost Optimization Strategies The main idea of this blog is to explain how organizations can reduce cloud costs when running Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS. The article focuses on practical ways to optimize infrastructure, improve resource usage, and make cloud deployments more efficient without losing reliability.
Main Point Running Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS can bring many benefits, but cost management is an important challenge. The blog shows that cost optimization should be considered from the beginning of the architecture design, not only after the system is already running. The solution approach is to apply cost-aware design choices such as better resource sizing, efficient service selection, and smarter usage of AWS capabilities.
Problems The blog highlights several common problems in cloud-based data platform deployments:
Cloud costs can grow quickly when services are over-provisioned. Poorly sized resources may waste money while still not improving performance. Teams may focus on functionality first and think about optimization later. Running systems at scale requires careful monitoring and planning to avoid unnecessary expenses. Solution Approach The proposed approach is to optimize the architecture and operations of Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS in a practical way. This includes choosing the right AWS services, using resources efficiently, and designing the system to match actual workload needs. The goal is to reduce unnecessary spending while keeping the platform reliable and scalable.
What I Can Learn From this blog, I can learn how to:
understand the importance of cost optimization in cloud architecture design systems that are efficient as well as functional improve my knowledge of AWS services and resource planning think more carefully about performance, scalability, and cost tradeoffs This topic is useful because it shows that good cloud engineering is not only about building systems, but also about making them sustainable and cost-effective.

Building a Scalable User Search Layer on Top of Amazon Cognito The main idea of this blog is to explain how to build a scalable user search layer on top of Amazon Cognito. The article focuses on solving the challenge of searching users efficiently when an application grows and the default Cognito capabilities are not enough for advanced lookup requirements.
Main Point Amazon Cognito is a strong identity service, but it does not natively provide the type of flexible and scalable user search experience that many applications need. The blog shows that a better approach is to build an additional search layer that works alongside Cognito so applications can search users more effectively while keeping the authentication system reliable.
Problems The blog highlights several important problems:
Amazon Cognito can handle authentication well, but searching users at scale can be difficult. Simple lookup requirements may be enough at first, but growing applications often need faster and more flexible search behavior. Relying only on native Cognito features may not support advanced search scenarios well. Applications often need a way to search users efficiently without compromising security or system performance. Solution Approach The proposed solution is to build a dedicated search layer on top of Cognito. This layer can use additional services and architecture patterns to support scalable search operations while keeping the identity system intact. The goal is to improve user discovery and usability without replacing the core authentication features of Cognito.
What I Can Learn From this blog, I can learn how to:
understand the limits of Amazon Cognito for user search scenarios design additional architecture layers for scalability and usability improve my knowledge of authentication, search patterns, and cloud application design think about how to combine AWS services to solve real-world application needs This topic is useful because it shows how cloud applications often need more than one service working together to meet growing user and business requirements.

title: Introduction
content: Core Technologies: The system utilizes three core managed services: Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB. In this workshop, you will use two VPCs. Problem Statement Daily challenge features typically experience “burst traffic” (sudden spikes in user access during specific hours). Maintaining a traditional 24/7 server to handle this is resource-inefficient and costly. Objective The goal is to build a complete RESTful API capable of auto-scaling to handle sudden traffic spikes without the need to configure or manage servers. The system is designed to maximize cost savings, aiming for a budget of $0 by utilizing the AWS Free Tier , while ensuring API response times remain under 500ms.

content:
AWS Account An active AWS Account is required. It is highly recommended to use an IAM User with AdministratorAccess privileges rather than the root account for better security practices.
API Testing Tool: Install Postman to simulate client requests and test the API endpoints.
Development Environment: A basic text editor is sufficient, as the business logic (Node.js) will be written directly within the AWS Lambda Console.

title: Proposal
content:
Serverless Daily Challenge Score API A Basic AWS Serverless Backend for Real-Time Scoring and Leaderboards 1. Executive Summary This project proposes a basic serverless backend on AWS for a daily challenge application that stores and retrieves user scores. The solution uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB to provide a RESTful API for score submission and leaderboard retrieval. It is designed to handle burst traffic efficiently while keeping infrastructure costs low.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Daily challenge applications often experience sudden spikes in traffic during specific hours and very low traffic at other times. Maintaining a traditional 24/7 server-based architecture would waste resources and increase operating costs. In addition, the development team wants to focus on UI/UX design and user experience rather than spending time managing servers and network infrastructure.
The Solution The proposed solution uses a fully serverless architecture. Client requests are sent via HTTP to Amazon API Gateway, which invokes AWS Lambda functions to process business logic. Lambda then stores or retrieves data in Amazon DynamoDB. The system provides two core endpoints:
POST /score: Submit a user score GET /leaderboard: Retrieve the top 10 highest scores This architecture is lightweight, cost-effective, and automatically scales based on demand.
3. Solution Architecture The architecture follows an event-driven model:
Client (Mobile/Web) → Amazon API Gateway → AWS Lambda → Amazon DynamoDB
Lambda also sends logs to Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and troubleshooting.
AWS Services Used Amazon API Gateway: Exposes secure RESTful API endpoints. AWS Lambda: Executes business logic in Node.js or Python. Amazon DynamoDB: Stores score records and supports fast read/write operations. Amazon CloudWatch: Collects logs and metrics for monitoring. 4. Technical Implementation The implementation is designed as a simple serverless backend with one database table and two API routes.
Core Components API Layer: Amazon API Gateway exposes public endpoints for score submission and leaderboard retrieval. Business Logic: AWS Lambda performs validation and handles score processing. Data Layer: Amazon DynamoDB stores user scores in a single table named DailyChallengeScores. Monitoring: CloudWatch Logs capture errors and latency, while alarms can be configured for API failures. Security and IAM Lambda uses an execution role with least-privilege permissions. The role is granted only the necessary permissions: dynamodb:PutItem and dynamodb:Query. DynamoDB is not exposed publicly and is accessed only through Lambda via AWS IAM. 5. Timeline & Milestones Week 1: Define project requirements, API endpoints, and the overall serverless architecture. Week 2: Set up the AWS environment, create the Lambda function, and configure API Gateway. Week 3: Design and create the DynamoDB table, then connect it to the Lambda function. Week 4: Implement API testing, security configuration, and basic monitoring with CloudWatch. Week 5: Deploy the solution, validate endpoint behavior, and finalize documentation and reporting. 6. Budget Estimation The system is expected to use AWS Free Tier as the primary cost model:
AWS Lambda: 1 million requests per month free Amazon DynamoDB: 25 GB storage free API Gateway: 1 million API calls per month free Estimated monthly cost: $0
7. Risk Assessment Risks CORS misconfiguration on API Gateway may prevent the frontend from calling the API. Missing IAM permissions may block Lambda from writing to DynamoDB and result in AccessDenied errors. Mitigation Strategies Configure CORS properly on API Gateway. Assign least-privilege IAM permissions to the Lambda execution role. Test integration thoroughly before deployment. 8. Expected Outcomes The project will deliver a lightweight, scalable, and low-cost backend for daily challenge applications. It will enable real-time score submission and leaderboard retrieval while allowing the development team to focus on frontend experience and product design.

This section lists the blogs I have posted so far. Each entry summarizes the main idea of the article and what I learned from it.
Blog 1 - Building Multi-Region Resiliency for AWS CloudFormation Custom Resource Deployment This blog explains how CloudFormation custom resources can be made more reliable across multiple AWS Regions by using resilient design patterns, safe retries, and failover strategies.
Blog 2 - Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS: Cost Optimization Strategies This blog focuses on how to reduce cloud costs when running Eclipse Dataspace Components on AWS by improving architecture decisions and resource efficiency.
Blog 3 - Building a Scalable User Search Layer on Top of Amazon Cognito This blog discusses how to build a scalable user search experience on top of Amazon Cognito so applications can handle growing user lookup needs more effectively.

title: Initialize the Database
content:
Create DynamoDB Table Access DynamoDB and create a new table named DailyChallengeScores.
Configure the Partition key as challengeId (String) and the Sort key as score (Number).
Select the On-demand capacity mode (Default settings) to optimize costs, paying only for actual read/write operations.

title: Configure Strict Permissions
content:
Create a JSON Policy Search IAM on search bar then open.
Access IAM and create a JSON Policy that grants only the minimum required permissions: dynamodb:PutItem, dynamodb:Query, and logs:CreateLogStream.
Set Policy name and create. Create a new IAM Role Create a new IAM Role specifically for AWS Lambda and attach the newly created Policy. This ensures secure interaction with the database without hard-coding access keys. Return to IAM and choose Roles, then choose Create role. Select AWS Service and choose Lambda. Add permission we just create above and set Role name and create. Add permission AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole for avoiding errors about CloudWatch Logs.

title: Set Up Amazon API Gateway
content: Create a new REST API Search api on search bar and choose API Gateway. Choose Create API and create REST API Add API name, choose Reginal and Create. After create API, on the left bar choose create resource. Add resource name and create. Configure POST and GET method Choose resource we just create and create method Create POST method Do the same with GET method using Lambda GetLeaderboardFunction. Enable CORS Return to resource and enable CORS. Deploy the API to a stage Return to resource and choose Deploy API. After deploy, get Invoke Url for later use.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The working environment was friendly, professional, and supportive. I had the chance to learn in a positive atmosphere where questions were welcomed and collaboration was encouraged. The environment helped me focus better and feel more confident during the learning process.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
The mentor and admin team were very helpful throughout the internship. They provided clear guidance, shared useful knowledge, and created opportunities for me to practice independently. I especially appreciated that they did not only give answers, but also encouraged me to think and solve problems by myself.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
The work was highly relevant to my academic background in information technology and software development. I was able to apply concepts from cloud computing, system design, and software development while also learning new topics such as serverless architecture, APIs, and modern AI applications.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
This internship helped me improve many important skills, especially cloud architecture, API development, teamwork, communication, and problem-solving. I also gained more confidence in presenting ideas and learning from real-world examples shared during the workshops and events.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
The company culture was positive and professional. People respected each other, worked seriously, and still maintained a friendly atmosphere. This made me feel comfortable and motivated to contribute, even as an intern.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship?
The most satisfying part was being able to complete a real project and see how the concepts I learned in the worklog and proposal could be applied in practice. I also enjoyed joining the events, where I learned about cloud careers, voice AI, and agentic AI in a very engaging way.
What do you think the company should improve for future interns?
I think the company could provide even more structured onboarding at the beginning, along with more practical examples and guided project materials for interns.
If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they intern here? Why or why not?
Yes, I would recommend it. The program offers a strong learning environment, supports personal growth, and gives interns a chance to explore real cloud and AI technologies in a professional setting.
Suggestions & Expectations I suggest keeping the internship experience practical and hands-on, while also providing more opportunities for interns to present their ideas and projects. I would like to continue being involved in similar programs in the future because they provide valuable exposure to the industry. Overall, this internship gave me a deeper understanding of cloud technology, teamwork, and professional growth, and I am grateful for the experience.

title: System Testing
content:
Test with Lambda Go to Lambda and choose SubmitScoreFunction. Go to test tab and create test then run test. Go check DynamoDB table. Choose explore items table. Go test with GetLeaderboardFunction. Test with PostMan Use Postman to send an HTTP POST request to the API URL with a JSON body to verify that an HTTP 200 response is returned. Send an HTTP GET request to verify that the API accurately returns the array of scores from DynamoDB.
Monitor the execution history and catch any potential errors using Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

title: Resource Clean-up
content:
After completing this workshop, to avoid any unexpected charges, delete the REST API in API Gateway, the two Lambda functions, the DynamoDB table, and the IAM Role and Policy to keep the environment clean.
Delete API Gateway Open API Gatewyat, choose api and delete. Delete Lambda Functions Open Lambda, choose funtions and delete. Delete DynamoDB Table Open DynamoDB, choose table and delete. Delete IAM Role and IAM Policy Open IAM, choose role and delete. Go to Policy tab and delete.
